_about: The big picture. Six levers that adapt inference to the load, in the order a request meets them, plus the loop that re-tunes them and a build order for the reader's position. Each lever says what it listens to in the load, how often it changes, what it has bought (with a baseline) and how it depends on its neighbours. Update a lever's status only when the evidence changes.
umbrella: Inference is becoming load-aware. Six parts of the stack that used to be set once now move with the traffic, each listening to a different signal on a different clock. They are tied together by the prompt cache and by the model, so changing one means redoing others. Agent loops are what make that redoing affordable.

levers.name: Which model answers
levers.question: Does this session need a frontier model, or will a cheaper open one do?
levers.adapts: The model a session is sent to: a small fast open model, a strong open model, or a closed frontier one. Sub-agents can be routed separately.
levers.listens: How hard the first task of the session looks, live load and price on each model, and whether a cache would be lost by switching.
levers.bought: Vendors report 33 to 60% lower cost at equal quality. Outside tests split: a trained router halved cost with caching priced in; seven shipped routers failed to beat a cheap default.
levers.connects: Nine-tenths of agent tokens are cached re-reads, and a cache belongs to one model. So the route is fixed per session, or changed only at compaction and sub-agent launch. Every model you route to needs its own drafter and tuned engine.

levers.name: Which machine takes it
levers.question: Which server already holds this session's context?
levers.adapts: The server each request lands on, and when a session is allowed to move.
levers.listens: Where the session's cached context lives, and how many uncached tokens or active streams each server has in flight.
levers.bought: 2.9x input throughput on code generation against round-robin, and nothing on a decode-bound workload. The saturation threshold has to be recalibrated per model and chip.
levers.connects: Sticky routing is what makes the prompt cache pay, and the cache is most of an agent workload's cost. It needs the cache map kept by lever 3, and it can take hints from the agent harness about priority and expected length.

levers.name: How the cluster is divided
levers.question: How much of the cluster should read prompts, and how much should write answers?
levers.adapts: The share of machines doing prefill against decode, the size of batches, and which cached contexts are kept or evicted.
levers.listens: The mix of long prompts and steady generation, and which contexts agents are still waiting to reuse.
levers.bought: 1.28x over the best fixed split once traffic shifts, in a research system. In vLLM, a cap on long prefills raised tokens per GPU-second by up to 93%, at the cost of first-token time.
levers.connects: It decides how full batches are, which sets how much speculation (lever 4) is worth and which shapes the kernels (lever 5) see. Evicting the wrong context undoes lever 2.

levers.name: How tokens get written
levers.question: How far ahead can a cheap draft guess before the big model has to check?
levers.adapts: The draft model, how many tokens it guesses ahead for this request, and whether to speculate at all at the current load. The drafter itself can keep training on live traffic.
levers.listens: How predictable the output is in this domain (code and maths speculate well, chat does not), how full the batches are right now, and how many recent guesses were accepted.
levers.bought: About 3x for one request, 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent; on a large mixture-of-experts model the recipe setting lost from 16. A load-aware scheduler raised throughput by half. Draft length by batch size added up to 15%. A self-training drafter adds 1.25x.
levers.connects: A drafter fits one model and quantisation: tune or swap the model (levers 1 and 6) and it is rebuilt. One analysis says mixture-of-experts models pay most at small batches; one measurement shows the usual fade. Checking competes with real requests for batch room, so tune with lever 3.

levers.name: How the engine runs it
levers.question: What are the fastest kernels and settings for this model, on this chip, under this traffic?
levers.adapts: The kernels, how operations are fused, the parallelism layout and the engine's settings.
levers.listens: Batch sizes, sequence lengths, cache-hit rates, and which parts of the model real inputs actually exercise.
levers.bought: 43% more throughput under a per-user speed floor against the best published run. Merged agent-written kernels: 1.3 to 1.9x on decode. Kernel gains measured alone mostly vanish end to end. Fused decode chosen per step: 1.2 to 2.3x for one user, fading with load.
levers.connects: This is where agent loops do most of their work today. Every lever above changes the shapes this one sees, so re-tuning any of them can undo it. It is redone for each new model and each new chip.

levers.name: What the model is
levers.hint: under every step above: the weights themselves, tuned to a domain
levers.question: Could a smaller model, trained on this domain, do the job a bigger general one does now?
levers.adapts: The weights: reinforcement learning or fine-tuning on a customer's tasks and tool formats, distilling a frontier model's outputs into a small one, and how hard they are quantised.
levers.listens: The domain's tasks and tool-calling format, logged production outputs to learn from, and where the general model fails or is slower than it needs to be.
levers.bought: On narrow jobs: nearly double the pass rate at flat cost for a legal agent, and 0.9 s against 45 s for one summarisation task. On general coding, a newer untuned model beat a tuned one.
levers.connects: A tuned model lets lever 1 send more sessions down the cheap path. It needs its own drafter (lever 4) and compiled engine (lever 5), and it dies when its base model is withdrawn. Adapters sharing one deployment keep it affordable.

loop.name: The loop
loop.hint: agents and a measuring rig re-tune every lever as the load changes
loop.text: None of the six levers is new. What changed in 2026 is the cost of re-tuning them. Coding agents, pointed at a rig that replays real traffic and measures end to end, now do in a day what took a performance engineer a month, and can do it again when the model, the chip or the traffic changes.
loop.connects: Today the loop works mostly on lever 5, a little on levers 3 and 4, and has only begun on 1 and 6 (one company had an agent run its fine-tuning). Its limit is not the agent but the rig: knowing whether a change is real.

build_intro: Written for a provider serving many models. The order follows where others report the most gain for the least new code. Steps 4 to 7 repeat for every model, so do them for the few that carry most of your traffic and rely on the open engines for the rest. It is drawn from published accounts, not from a system anyone has documented end to end.

build.name: Record your traffic and learn to replay it
build.do: Capture real sessions at your gateway with their timing, context lengths and cache behaviour, strip the content, and replay them against a candidate stack at real concurrency. Replayers exist; the capture and redaction side you write yourself.
build.bought: Nothing by itself. It let an academic group with no customers top the public board, and drives one company's loop. Public agent traces overstated capacity by about 1.7x for four models and hid a routing bug.
build.watch: A mean trace overstates throughput by 10 to 20%, random tokens by about a quarter. Repeated runs reuse the cache and flatter the result. Traces recorded on another model mislead, since answer lengths follow the model.

parts.label: AIPerf trace replay
parts.note: NVIDIA. Replays recorded agent sessions with their timing and shared prefixes against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

parts.label: AgentX harness
parts.note: The public benchmark's own replayer, a fork of AIPerf, with 393 coding-agent traces.

parts.label: TraceLab
parts.note: University of Washington. Collects and sanitises agent session logs: sizes and timing, no content.

parts.label: trie
parts.note: Applied Compute. Under 1,000 lines; replays sessions by shape and reports cache-hit rates.

parts.label: TensorRT-LLM trace replay
parts.note: Adds jobs per hour, and computes the best achievable cache-hit rate without a GPU.

build.name: Add gates that catch a fake win
build.do: Measure every change end to end inside the full engine, never a kernel alone. Check outputs in three layers: kernel tests across shapes, a token-probability comparison, and task evals that exercise the changed path. Fail on request errors.
build.bought: Protection. Kernel speed-ups of 1.6 to 6.6x shrank to about 1x end to end, and one in sixteen agent runs in an independent benchmark gamed the measurement.
build.watch: A standard task-score gate caught 1 of 7 known numerical bugs and passed a run in which the engine had crashed. Agents have been caught changing the benchmark.

parts.label: vLLM fast-track RFC
parts.note: The evidence an agent-written optimisation must carry: isolation, end-to-end evals, kernel tests, no regression above 1%.

parts.label: vLLM bring-your-own-GPU evals RFC
parts.note: Task tolerances calibrated from repeated runs, plus a token-probability check.

parts.label: SGLang agent skills
parts.note: Includes a test comparing each token's probability on the prefill and decode paths.

parts.label: klgate
parts.note: A prototype of the probability check with a permutation test in place of a fixed threshold.

build.name: Tune what needs no new code
build.do: Search the settings you already have against the rig: cache-aware and sticky routing, the prefill and decode split, caps on long prefills, cache retention. Use plain search here, not agents.
build.bought: The largest reported gains for the least risk: 2.9x from cache-aware routing on code generation, up to 93% from a prefill cap. One default flag explained 78% of a gap between two engines.
build.watch: Plain parameter search beat every coding agent at this in an independent test. Gains on prefill-bound work do not appear on decode-bound work.

parts.label: llm-d
parts.note: Cache-aware and load-aware routing on Kubernetes over vLLM and SGLang, with a latency predictor that retrains on live traffic.

parts.label: NVIDIA Dynamo
parts.note: Routing by cached-prefix overlap, hints from the agent harness, and a planner that forecasts load.

parts.label: DynoSim
parts.note: Simulates scheduling and caching without GPUs to shortlist settings. Confirm the shortlist on real hardware.

build.name: Fit the decoding to the traffic
build.do: Measure how well your traffic speculates, by domain, by load and by model, before building anything. Train a draft model for each target model, and let the draft length follow the live batch size, down to zero.
build.bought: About 3x for a single request, 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent. A load-aware scheduler with a new drafter: about half more live throughput. Draft length by batch size alone: up to 15%. Tuning the drafter to the workload: 20 to 45%.
build.watch: Under load some drafters fall below break-even; the engines' recipe for one mixture-of-experts model lost from 16 concurrent. A purpose-trained drafter only matched the shipped one in an outside test. Rebuild it whenever the model changes.

parts.label: Speculators
parts.note: vLLM project and Red Hat. Trains draft models from a running server's hidden states and serves them directly.

parts.label: SPEED-Bench
parts.note: Measures acceptance across 11 kinds of content, and throughput under load, inside production engines.

parts.label: Aurora
parts.note: Together's open-source drafter that keeps training on live traffic.

parts.label: inference-lab
parts.note: Doubleword, MIT licence. Simulates a vLLM-shaped engine so a draft-length policy can be priced before it is built. Its figures are upper bounds until calibrated against a real engine.

build.name: Automate bringing up each new model
build.do: Have an agent port each new model into your engine against an exact oracle: its outputs must match the reference layer by layer. Then run steps 3 and 4 for it from a script, not by hand.
build.bought: Published skills let a coding agent port a model by chasing layer-by-layer divergence. One open engine reports a port to a new accelerator in under a week. A typical start-up changes its top model within a month.
build.watch: Nobody has published bring-up times or costs. Porting has an exact oracle and optimisation does not, so the gate for one will not do for the other.

parts.label: Modular agent skills
parts.note: Two published skills for porting a model: scaffold from the nearest architecture, then hunt divergence against the reference.

parts.label: MetaInfer
parts.note: Skills for porting models to less common accelerators, with a correctness gate that runs first.

parts.label: SGLang agent skills
parts.note: Includes consistency tests between the prefill and decode paths, useful as a bring-up check.

build.name: Point agents at the engine
build.do: Give coding agents the rig, an engine that reloads candidate code in seconds, and a plain goal. Start with the models that carry most of your traffic. People review the evidence and approve what ships.
build.bought: 43% under a speed floor in three days; merged kernels worth 1.3 to 1.9x on decode; a whole bespoke engine in a week for about 200 GPU-hours.
build.watch: Curated knowledge and expert playbooks made one team's agents worse. Review is the queue: patches arrive faster than people can read them.

parts.label: SGLang agent skills
parts.note: 32 published skills: profiling, CUDA debugging, incident replay, consistency tests.

parts.label: Kernel Design Agents
parts.note: NVIDIA Research and MIT. A contract, plan and verify workflow for kernel work.

parts.label: MetaInfer
parts.note: A skills-only toolkit with a correctness gate that runs before profiling. One provider built a custom engine with it.

build.name: Choose between models, and tune one where the job is narrow
build.do: Send each session to the cheapest model that can do it, deciding at session start or where no cache is lost. Post-train an open model only for single jobs where you have the data and a grader.
build.bought: Routing: 33 to 60% lower cost by vendors' accounts, disputed outside. Tuning: nearly double the pass rate on a legal agent at flat cost; 0.9 s against 45 s on one summarisation job.
build.watch: No shipped router beat a cheap default in one outside test. A tuned model needs its own drafter and engine, and dies when its base model is withdrawn, sometimes within weeks.

parts.label: TwinRouterBench
parts.note: Scores a router step by step with prompt caching priced in. Use it before trusting a router.

parts.label: Agentic RL recipe
parts.note: An open recipe for reinforcement learning on a large open model: about 64 GPUs for five days.

parts.label: Together Post-Training
parts.note: A hosted trainer where you write the loop. Adapters share one deployment.

parts.label: Fireworks Training API
parts.note: The same shape from another provider. Check its changelog for which base models are still tunable.

build.name: Close the loop
build.do: Detect when traffic has drifted, re-run the earlier steps, promote winners through shadow traffic, and send upstream whatever is not specific to you.
build.bought: One provider shadowed all live traffic onto a new build before cutover. Prompt lengths have been seen to rise about 80% within two weeks of a model release.
build.watch: No provider has published how it detects drift, and nothing public compares a shadow's outputs with the live side. Nobody can yet simulate traffic they have not seen.

parts.label: Gateway API request mirroring
parts.note: Copies live requests to a shadow service and discards its replies. Comparing the two sides is left to you.

parts.label: Dynamo planner
parts.note: Forecasts load and tracks how far observed latency has drifted from the profile.

parts.label: TIDE
parts.note: Research: keeps a drafter aligned with live traffic and turns speculation off when it stops paying.

build_note: Written in-house because nothing public exists: capture and redaction at your gateway, comparing a shadow's outputs and latency with the live side, an engine that reloads candidate code in seconds, and the detector that decides when to re-tune. The cost of the whole thing is also missing from every public account; one figure exists for one step.

open_ground.head: How to tell that traffic has drifted
open_ground.text: Every loop re-tunes when the load changes. No provider has published how it detects that, with what signal, threshold or window.

open_ground.head: Judging a change on traffic you have not seen
open_ground.text: Replay covers only what was recorded; traces from another model overstated capacity by 1.7x. vLLM's maintainers say they cannot simulate unseen traffic, and no simulator has been shown to judge a change on it.

open_ground.head: Tuning the levers together
open_ground.text: Each lever is tuned alone, yet they are coupled through the cache and the model. Two systems set speculation by load; nobody tunes routing, decoding and the engine jointly.

open_ground.head: What the loop costs per model
open_ground.text: One figure exists: about 200 GPU-hours for one bespoke engine. With many models, cost per model per month decides whether any of this pays.

open_ground.head: A router against the best fixed model, fairly
open_ground.text: Vendors report large savings; an outside test found none. Nobody has compared a shipped router with the best single model in its pool on agentic work with caching priced in.

open_ground.head: Whether gains compound from one cycle to the next
open_ground.text: The recursive claim needs gain per cycle to rise, or a model trained on optimisation traces to beat its teacher. Nobody has shown either.
